profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting at an outpatient behavioral medicine clinic affiliated with a university hospital. The team is reviewing a proposed single-case experimental design for evaluating a brief sleep-restriction and stimulus-control intervention in adults with chronic insomnia who are already receiving routine CBT-I-informed care. The draft protocol is intended to function as a clinic-embedded practice-improvement project and, if methodologically sound, support later publication as a small case series using single-case logic. The proposal describes a 'multiple-baseline single-case protocol' with daily sleep diaries, weekly clinician ratings, and actigraphy on selected participants. Agenda: assess whether the design as written supports credible individual-level inference, determine whether baseline monitoring and treatment transition rules are workable in ordinary clinic flow, and decide what revisions are needed before approval. Expected outcome: conditional approval with a short design addendum that preserves clinic feasibility while clarifying the protocol sufficiently for implementation.

members.name: Dr. Elena Park
members.role: Clinical Psychologist and Behavioral Sleep Program Lead
members.expertise: CBT-I, outpatient intervention design, routine outcome monitoring, ethical implementation in clinical settings
members.background: Dr. Park directs the hospital's behavioral sleep service and supervises clinicians delivering brief insomnia interventions in a high-throughput outpatient setting; she has used structured symptom tracking in practice but has limited formal training in formal single-case experimental methodology beyond applied workshops.
members.private_state: She wants the protocol approved quickly so it can be integrated into clinic workflows next month without creating rigid procedures that therapists will resist or that could delay treatment for distressed patients; she is especially attentive to patient acceptability and clinician autonomy.
hidden_assumptions: A protocol can still legitimately be called a multiple-baseline design if patients have pretreatment monitoring and begin treatment at naturally different calendar times because of intake and scheduling variation.
A baseline is stable enough when the therapist can see a clinically coherent pattern after a few diary days, even if there is no explicit numerical rule.
If the team says they will refine operational details during the pilot, that means they can work out the practical decision rules in response to what actually happens in clinic.

When everyone agrees the study team will monitor baseline, the treating therapist is the obvious person to do that because they already review the diary with the patient and are responsible for treatment timing.
Minor operational flexibility to shorten or transition phases in response to engagement or symptom concerns does not fundamentally alter the design's clinical usefulness.

members.name: Dr. Marcus Levin
members.expertise: Single-case experimental designs, causal inference in small-N studies, measurement schedules, protocol standardization for publishable clinical research
members.background: Dr. Levin supports embedded research across the hospital and has published methodological papers on multiple-baseline and withdrawal designs in behavioral health settings; he is frequently asked to review clinic-originated protocols before IRB or quality-improvement submission.
members.private_state: He wants the clinic to use a design that will survive methodological scrutiny and not become ordinary care with a research label attached; he is willing to accommodate clinic realities, but only if the inferential logic remains intact and reproducible.
hidden_assumptions: A multiple-baseline design requires intentionally staggered baseline lengths or phase onsets determined by a prespecified plan rather than by ordinary scheduling differences alone.
Baseline stability should be judged by explicit repeated-measure criteria, typically with enough observations to assess level, trend, and variability before a phase change.

If the team says details will be refined during the pilot, that means the rules are already prespecified in draft form and the pilot is only checking feasibility and adherence, not inventing the rules case by case.
When people say the study team will monitor baseline, that ordinarily implies a centralized reviewer such as a coordinator, PI, or methods lead applying the same rule across cases.
Ad hoc therapist-controlled transition decisions change the level of inference the design can support even if the intervention remains clinically appropriate.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a multiple-baseline design
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to the proposal as a 'multiple-baseline' design.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means that each patient will complete some pretreatment monitoring and will begin treatment at naturally different times because referrals, intake completion, and scheduling differ across patients.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means that baseline lengths or treatment onsets will be deliberately staggered across cases according to a prespecified sequence so the offset itself contributes to causal inference.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The draft already uses the term 'multiple-baseline,' and both participants are accustomed to hearing it as a settled label; because they are discussing refinements rather than arguing over naming, neither initially feels compelled to restate the methodological core.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that treatment should begin once the baseline is 'stable.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means that after roughly 3-4 nightly diary entries the patient's sleep pattern looks clinically consistent enough for the therapist to start the intervention without unnecessary delay.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means that baseline should meet an explicit rule, such as at least 5-7 observations with limited trend and acceptable variability on target sleep measures before phase transition.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In both clinical and research settings, 'stable baseline' sounds like a standard safeguard rather than a contested threshold; the divergence lies in the evidentiary bar behind the phrase, not in the phrase itself.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to 'refine the details during the pilot'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that some details can be 'refined during the pilot phase.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 presupposes this means the team can discover and settle practical rules during early rollout—for example, how to handle missed sleep diaries, when to allow an early transition after a bad week, or how therapists phrase adherence reminders—based on what proves workable with actual patients.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 presupposes this means the operational rules will already be written into the addendum and the pilot will only test whether those prewritten rules are feasible to execute consistently, not generate them on the fly.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Saying details will be refined in a pilot is common project language and normally signals sensible pragmatism rather than a disagreement about whether the rules already exist; each person hears the phrase through their own standard institutional practice and assumes shared understanding.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that 'the study team will monitor the baseline.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes each treating therapist will review the patient's diary trajectory at the weekly visit and decide when baseline has run its course, since the therapist already manages the case and knows when waiting longer is clinically awkward.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes a centralized reviewer—such as the project coordinator or methods lead—will check incoming diary data against the protocol and authorize the phase transition in the same way across cases.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both interpretations sound like ordinary study-team oversight, and neither participant sees their version as a special procedural choice worth foregrounding; the ambiguity hides in the locus of control behind the collective phrase 'study team.'

turns.inner_thought: I want to get this approved with only a light addendum. As far as I'm concerned, this already qualifies as a multiple-baseline design because each patient will have pretreatment monitoring and people will move into treatment at different times through ordinary clinic flow. The important thing is to keep it usable next month and not burden therapists with research-style rigidity.
turns.utterance: Thanks for joining. What I'd like to do today is confirm that the insomnia protocol is ready for approval as a multiple-baseline single-case design that can sit inside routine clinic care without creating unnecessary drag for patients or therapists.

turns.inner_thought: The concept is workable, but I need to make sure this doesn't end up being ordinary care with a research label. If we're going to call it a single-case multiple-baseline project and possibly publish it later, the inferential logic has to hold up. I'll stay collaborative and push for enough structure to make it reproducible.
turns.utterance: Overall, I think the plan is promising. My main interest is making sure it supports credible within-patient inference while still fitting the realities of clinic operations.

turns.inner_thought: The practical advantage is that we don't need artificial scheduling. Referrals come in unevenly, patients finish intake at different rates, and clinicians have different openings, so the baselines will naturally differ in timing. That is plenty for what we need, and it avoids delaying care just to satisfy a design ideal.
turns.utterance: From the clinic side, we can stagger the baselines according to the intake schedule. Referrals, paperwork completion, and appointment availability already vary, so treatment starts won't all line up, which gives us the multiple-baseline structure we're after.

turns.inner_thought: Good, they are thinking in terms of a stagger. If it's tied to the intake schedule, I can work with that so long as the first cases are organized in a prespecified way rather than left entirely to happenstance. I don't need to spell that out right now; I can just steer us toward writing it down in the addendum.
turns.utterance: Yes, that seems workable. For the first several cases, I'd just want that stagger reflected clearly in the addendum so the sequence is easy to follow when we review the cases later.

turns.inner_thought: What matters in practice is not keeping people waiting. If the diary looks coherent after three or four nights, that's stable enough to begin; only very erratic cases need longer. I need to present this as standard clinical judgment rather than a contentious threshold.
turns.utterance: Agreed. The practical plan is to begin treatment once the baseline is stable, and in most cases I expect that to happen fairly quickly unless someone's sleep pattern is unusually erratic.

turns.inner_thought: Stable baseline is the right concept, but for me that means an explicit repeated-measures rule, ideally enough observations to assess level, trend, and variability on core targets like sleep efficiency and wake after sleep onset. If they can put that in writing, the design becomes defensible.
turns.utterance: That sounds reasonable. I think the key will be to specify in the write-up how we're defining a stable baseline for the main sleep targets before the phase change occurs.

turns.inner_thought: The study team monitoring the baseline obviously means the treating therapist reviewing the diary in the weekly session and deciding when it's settled enough to move forward. I don't want some separate reviewer creating bottlenecks or forcing patients to wait when the clinician can already see the pattern.
turns.utterance: Yes, and the simplest way to handle that is that the study team will monitor the baseline during the weekly reviews and move forward once the pattern looks settled.

turns.inner_thought: Good—that gives me an opening to formalize a centralized, consistent review process in the addendum. When I hear 'study team will monitor the baseline,' I take that to mean a standard oversight function applying the same transition logic across cases. As long as we capture that, we can keep the clinic burden modest.
turns.utterance: I think that's fine. It would help to capture that monitoring process in the addendum so the study team is applying the same transition logic consistently across cases.

turns.inner_thought: We really should not try to script every contingency before launch. The real clinic problems—missed diary nights, wavering engagement, awkward timing questions, how much flexibility to allow—are best worked out once we start using the protocol. That's exactly what I mean by refining the details during the pilot phase.
turns.utterance: From my perspective, the major pieces are already there. The remaining items—things like missed-diary handling and a few edge cases—can be refined during the pilot phase once the clinic starts using the protocol.

turns.inner_thought: A pilot is appropriate if the procedures are already drafted and we're testing whether the team can carry them out reliably. I hear 'refined during the pilot phase' as feasibility checking and modest adjustment, not inventing rules case by case. I'll affirm the pilot while keeping it framed as implementation of specified procedures.
turns.utterance: I agree a pilot makes sense. It will be useful to see whether those procedures are workable in practice once the team begins implementing them.

turns.inner_thought: If we keep this recognizable but flexible, therapists will actually adopt it. I need room for clinicians to respond to patient circumstances, adjust pacing when needed, and avoid feeling policed by a rigid protocol, while still sounding methodologically respectable.
turns.utterance: Exactly. What I'm hoping is that this preserves clinical flexibility while still keeping the design recognizable and manageable for therapists in day-to-day care.

turns.inner_thought: I can support this if the addendum nails down the essentials as I understand them: the multiple-baseline stagger as a planned feature, a clear stable-baseline criterion, and a monitoring procedure the pilot will test for consistent use. That should make the project methodologically defensible without overbuilding it.
turns.utterance: In that case, my recommendation would be conditional approval pending a brief addendum that specifies the multiple-baseline stagger, the baseline stability criterion, and the monitoring procedure the pilot will operationalize.
